ARTICLE 2: OBJECTS AND FUNCTIONS

2.1 The principal objects of the Union shall be:

(a) To promote the economic and social welfare of its members through cooperative enterprise, mutual aid, and the equitable sharing of benefits derived from the collective activities of the Union.

(b) To act as an umbrella body for primary cooperative societies operating within the Benue River Basin, providing them with coordination, representation, and support in their dealings with government, financial institutions, and commercial buyers.

(c) To organise the collective purchase of inputs, including improved seeds, fertiliser, agrochemicals, and fishing gear, at wholesale prices for distribution to member societies.

(d) To establish and operate storage facilities, including silos, cold rooms, and drying floors, for the preservation of members' produce and to reduce post-harvest losses.

(e) To facilitate access to credit for members through the maintenance of a revolving loan fund and through negotiations with commercial banks and microfinance institutions.

(f) To engage in the processing and marketing of agricultural and aquatic products, including rice, yam, cassava, maize, soybeans, fish, and other commodities produced by members.

(g) To provide training and extension services to members in modern farming techniques, financial management, cooperative governance, and environmental stewardship.

(h) To undertake such other activities as may be conducive to the attainment of the foregoing objects, including the acquisition of land, vehicles, and equipment necessary for the Union's operations.

(b) The principle of democratic control, whereby each member society shall have one vote, regardless of its size or financial contribution.

(c) The principle of limited interest on share capital, and the equitable distribution of surplus among members in proportion to their transactions with the Union.

ARTICLE 1: NAME, HEADQUARTERS, AND SEAL

1.1 The name of the Union shall be the Benue River Basin Cooperative Union, hereinafter referred to as "the Union."

The headquarters shall be the principal place of business and the registered office of the Union, where the central records, registers, and seal of the Union shall be kept, unless otherwise directed by the Council for reasons of security or operational necessity.

1.3 The Union shall have a common seal, which shall be kept in the custody of the Secretary General and shall not be used except by the authority of the Council, and every instrument to which the seal is affixed shall be countersigned by the Secretary General and the Treasurer or by two other members of the Council as the Council may from time to time appoint.

1.4 The Union may establish branch offices, depots, or service centres in any part of Benue State or elsewhere in Nigeria, as the General Meeting may determine upon the recommendation of the Council. The establishment of any such branch shall not alter the location of the headquarters as provided in Section 1.2.

---

ARTICLE 2: OBJECTS AND POWERS

2.1 The objects of the Union shall be:
(a) to promote the economic and social welfare of its member societies and their members;
(b) to provide a common platform for the procurement of inputs, the marketing of produce, and the provision of credit and savings facilities;
(c) to organise, coordinate, and supervise the activities of member societies in accordance with cooperative principles;
(d) to provide training, extension, and advisory services to member societies;
(e) to establish and maintain such facilities and enterprises as may be necessary or expedient for the attainment of the foregoing objects;
(f) to act as an agent of the government or of any agency, corporate or otherwise, for the purpose of implementing programmes of agricultural development, rural development, or cooperative development.

2.2 In furtherance of its objects, the Union shall have power:
(a) to borrow money, whether on overdraft or otherwise, and to give security for any such borrowing;
(b) to acquire, hold, lease, or dispose of land, buildings, equipment, and other property;
(c) to enter into contracts and agreements with any person, firm, or corporate body;
(d) to invest its funds in such securities or enterprises as the General Meeting may approve;
(e) to sue and be sued in its own name.

---

ARTICLE 3: MEMBERSHIP

(Note: The provisions of this Article have been consolidated from the original 2012 text and the amendments of 2016 and 2019. Where a provision has been amended, the amended text governs.)

3.1 Membership of the Union shall be open to registered cooperative societies whose principal place of business is within the Benue River Basin area, and which are engaged in agriculture, including crop production, livestock, fishery, and related enterprises, or in the provision of services to agricultural producers.

3.2 Application for membership shall be made in writing to the Secretary General, accompanied by:
(a) a certified copy of the society's certificate of registration;
(b) a copy of the society's constitution and bylaws;
(c) the names and addresses of the society's authorised representatives;
(d) the prescribed admission fee and the minimum share capital subscription as determined by the General Meeting.
ARTICLE 4: VOTING, QUORUM, AND CONDUCT OF MEETINGS

(Note: This Article consolidates the original 2012 provisions with the amendments of 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2023. The text of each Section as set out below is the text currently in force.)

4.1 Right to Vote
(a) Each member society shall be entitled to one vote on every matter coming before the General Meeting, irrespective of the size of the society or the amount of its share capital.
(b) Voting shall be exercised by the authorised representative of the member society, whose name has been duly communicated to the Secretary General in accordance with Article 3.2(c).
(c) No member society shall be entitled to vote at any meeting if it is in arrears in the payment of any subscription, levy, or other sum due to the Union, provided that the Council of Delegates may, in its discretion and upon good cause shown, waive this disqualification for a particular meeting.
(d) Voting by proxy shall not be permitted. A member society unable to attend a meeting shall be deemed absent, and no other society or person may cast its vote.

4.2 Manner of Voting
(a) Voting shall ordinarily be by show of hands, unless a poll is demanded by the chairperson or by at least five member societies present and entitled to vote.
(b) Where a poll is demanded, it shall be taken by secret ballot in such manner as the chairperson may direct, and the result of the poll shall be declared by the chairperson and recorded in the minutes.
(c) For the election of officers and for any resolution amending this Constitution, voting shall be by secret ballot.
(d) A declaration by the chairperson that a resolution has been carried, or carried by a particular majority, shall be conclusive evidence of that fact, unless a poll is demanded in accordance with subsection (a) of this Section.

4.3 Quorum
(a) The quorum for a General Meeting shall be one-third of the member societies entitled to vote, present in person or by authorised representative.
(b) The quorum for a meeting of the Council of Delegates shall be one-half of the members of the Council.
(c) If within one hour after the time appointed for a meeting a quorum is not present, the meeting shall stand adjourned to the same day in the following week at the same time and place, or to such other day, time, and place as the chairperson may determine. At the adjourned meeting, the members present shall form a quorum, provided that not less than ten member societies are present.
(d) If at any meeting a quorum ceases to be present during the proceedings, the meeting may continue to receive reports and to adjourn, but shall not transact any other business.

4.4 Motions and Seconding
(a) No motion, other than a motion of procedure, shall be put to a meeting unless it has been seconded.
(b) A motion which is not seconded shall not be debated and shall be deemed to have lapsed.
(c) The proposer and the seconder of a motion shall be members entitled to vote at the meeting.
(d) An amendment to a motion may be moved, and if seconded, shall be debated and voted upon before the substantive motion is put.
(e) The chairperson may, with the consent of the meeting, accept a motion for the closure of debate. Such a motion shall be put to the meeting without debate and shall require a two-thirds majority of the votes cast.

4.5 Minutes and Records
(a) The Secretary General shall cause proper minutes to be kept of all proceedings of General Meetings and of meetings of the Council of Delegates.
(b) Minutes of each meeting shall be circulated to member societies within thirty days of the meeting, and shall be confirmed, amended, or rejected at the next meeting of the same body.
(c) A member society may, by written request to the Secretary General, have access to the minutes of any General Meeting, provided that the Council may restrict access to minutes or parts of minutes which, in its opinion, relate to matters of a confidential nature.
CONSTITUTION AND BYLAWS OF THE BENUE RIVER BASIN COOPERATIVE UNION

(Adopted at the Inaugural General Meeting, 14 April 2012; as amended through the
Extraordinary General Meeting of 18 March 2023)

---

ARTICLE 5: AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION AND BYLAWS

5.1 Right to Propose Amendments

(a) Any member society may propose an amendment to this Constitution or to the
Bylaws by submitting a written notice to the Secretary General at least sixty (60)
days before the date of the General Meeting at which the amendment is to be
considered.

(b) The Council of Delegates may likewise propose amendments, either on its own
initiative or upon the petition of not fewer than five member societies.

(c) Each proposal shall set out the exact wording of the article or section sought
to be amended, the reasons for the amendment, and the names and signatures of the
proposer and the seconder.

5.2 Circulation of Proposals

(a) Upon receipt of a valid proposal, the Secretary General shall circulate the
full text of the proposed amendment, together with the names of the proposer and
seconder, to all member societies not later than forty-five (45) days before the
General Meeting.

(b) The notice shall also indicate whether the Council of Delegates recommends
the adoption or rejection of the proposed amendment, or offers no recommendation.

(c) No amendment shall be considered at a General Meeting unless it has been
circulated in accordance with this section, unless the meeting by a two-thirds
majority of the votes cast suspends this requirement for reasons of urgency.

5.3 Adoption of Amendments

(a) An amendment to this Constitution shall be adopted only if it is approved by
a two-thirds majority of the votes cast by member societies present and voting at
a General Meeting.

(b) An amendment to the Bylaws shall require a simple majority of the votes
cast, except that an amendment to the Bylaws concerning the levying of dues or
the expulsion of a member society shall require a two-thirds majority.

(c) Voting shall be by secret ballot if so demanded by not fewer than one-third
of the member societies present.

(d) An amendment shall take effect immediately upon its adoption, unless the
resolution adopting it specifies a later date.

5.4 Review of the Constitution

(a) The Council of Delegates shall cause a full review of this Constitution and
the Bylaws to be undertaken at intervals of not more than five years.

(b) The review shall be conducted by a Constitution Review Committee appointed
by the Council, comprising not fewer than five persons, of whom at least three
shall be representatives of member societies.

(c) The Committee shall report to the Council, and the Council shall table the
report, together with its recommendations, at the next General Meeting.

5.5 Repeal and Replacement

(a) A proposal to repeal this Constitution and replace it with a new constitution
shall be treated as an amendment for the purposes of this Article, and shall
require a two-thirds majority of the votes cast at a General Meeting.

(b) The notice of such a proposal shall be accompanied by the full text of the
proposed new constitution.

---

ARTICLE 6: DISPUTE RESOLUTION

6.1 Objectives and Scope

(a) The Union shall seek to resolve all disputes arising between member
societies, between a member society and the Union, or between the Union and any
third party, by amicable means in the first instance.

(b) This Article shall not apply to disputes between individual members of a
member society, which shall be dealt with under the internal rules of that
society.

- The cooperative's bye-laws were reviewed and amendments were proposed to the membership committee for further action.
- Correspondence with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development regarding the cooperative's registration status was ongoing; the cooperative's registration certificate remains valid until December 2024.
- The secretariat processed 312 membership applications, of which 289 were approved.

The report noted that minutes of all meetings had been circulated to members within two weeks of each meeting, as required.

- Total expenditure: ₦41,920,300

- Savings and deposits held with the cooperative: ₦112,300,000 (unaudited figure as at 31 December 2022)

The Treasurer noted that the cooperative had maintained a savings-to-loan ratio of approximately 1.6 to 1, which was within the limits set by the bye-laws.

He also reported that the cooperative had received a grant of ₦2,500,000 from the Benue State Government for the purchase of improved cassava cuttings, which was received in November 2022 and was yet to be fully utilised.

**8.4 Report of the Assistant Treasurer**

Mr. Emeka Nwosu reported on the status of the cooperative's loan portfolio. As at 31 December 2022:

- Total loans disbursed during the year: ₦18,250,000
- Total loans repaid: ₦14,780,000
- Outstanding loans: ₦23,400,000 (including loans from previous years)
- Loans in arrears (over 90 days): ₦1,850,000, representing 7.9% of the outstanding portfolio

He noted that the loan recovery committee had intensified efforts to recover overdue loans, and that 12 defaulters had been issued final notices. The committee recommended that the cooperative consider writing off loans totalling ₦350,000 that were owed by three members who had died during the year and whose families were unable to repay.
**9. CONSIDERATION OF THE AUDITED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS**

The Chairman invited Mr. Uche to present the audited financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2022. Mr. Uche referred members to the copies that had been circulated with the notice of the meeting, and he read out the Auditor's Report, which gave an unqualified opinion.

Mr. Uche then highlighted the following key extracts:

Mrs. Grace Adah raised a question regarding the ₦350,000 loans recommended for write-off, asking whether the cooperative had exhausted all recovery avenues. The Loan Recovery Committee Chairman, Mr. Daniel Iorhemba, responded that the three deceased members' estates had been contacted, and letters of administration were either not being pursued or the families had indicated inability to pay. After lengthy debate, the meeting agreed that the write-off should proceed, subject to the approval of the bye-laws.

**3.1 Input Supply Programme**

The cooperative facilitated the bulk procurement and distribution of improved seed varieties, fertilizers, and agrochemicals to members. A total of 1,240 bags of NPK fertilizer, 850 bags of urea, and 3.2 metric tonnes of certified maize and soybean seed were distributed at subsidized rates through the union's input credit window. **3.2 Seed Store Construction**

The construction of the 500-metric-tonne central seed store was completed in September 2022. The facility, located adjacent to the Gboko main market, was funded through a combination of member levies (₦8.5 million), a BRBCU development grant (₦4.0 million), and a loan from the Benue State Agricultural Development Fund (₦3.2 million). The store has been commissioned and is currently being used to warehouse the 2022 dry-season harvest.

**3.3 Training and Extension**

In collaboration with the Benue State Agricultural Development Programme (BSADP), the cooperative organized four training workshops during the year. Topics included climate-smart agronomy, post-harvest loss reduction, and cooperative governance. A total of 312 members attended at least one of the workshops. A further 45 members completed a week-long farmer-to-farmer exchange visit to a cooperative in Makurdi.

**3.4 Marketing and Off-Take**

The cooperative entered into an off-take agreement with a regional grain aggregator for the sale of 600 metric tonnes of maize at a floor price of ₦185,000 per tonne. This arrangement provided members with a guaranteed market and reduced reliance on middlemen. The actual volume delivered under the agreement was 584 metric tonnes; the shortfall was due to a localized outbreak of fall armyworm affecting a small cluster of farms in the Tse-Agberagbe area.

A total of 1,450 tonnes of fresh cassava roots were processed at the cooperative's facilities. This yielded approximately 420 tonnes of gari and 180 tonnes of fufu flour. The remaining 2,200 tonnes of fresh roots were sold directly to local markets and to a midstream processor in Makurdi.

The cooperative also commenced a small-scale high-quality cassava flour (HQCF) pilot in October, processing 45 tonnes of roots into 15 tonnes of HQCF. The pilot was supported by a technical partner from Ibadan and the product is being test-marketed to a bakery in Lafia. Feedback from the bakery has been positive, and a full-scale rollout is being considered for 2023 subject to a market assessment.

**4.3 Livestock and Other Enterprises**

The cooperative's livestock component, which is a minor activity, reported a total of 120 goats and 45 pigs raised by 38 member households. A poultry unit established in early 2022 raised 1,200 broilers in two batches. The poultry unit recorded a net profit of ₦780,000 for the year, which was distributed to the participating members on a per-bird basis.

**4.4 Post-Harvest Losses**

Post-harvest losses across all crops were estimated at 8.5% of total production. The primary causes were improper drying during the wet season harvest and inadequate storage space before the completion of the seed store in September. The cooperative is targeting a reduction in losses to 5% in 2023 through the use of hermetic storage bags and the newly constructed store.

ARTICLE 2: OBJECTS AND FUNCTIONS

2.1 The principal objects of the Union shall be:

(a) To promote the economic and social welfare of its members through cooperative enterprise, mutual aid, and the equitable sharing of benefits derived from the collective activities of the Union.

(b) To act as an umbrella body for primary cooperative societies operating within the Benue River Basin, providing them with coordination, representation, and support in their dealings with government, financial institutions, and commercial buyers.

(c) To organise the collective purchase of inputs, including improved seeds, fertiliser, agrochemicals, and fishing gear, at wholesale prices for distribution to member societies.

(d) To establish and operate storage facilities, including silos, cold rooms, and drying floors, for the preservation of members' produce and to reduce post-harvest losses.

(e) To facilitate access to credit for members through the maintenance of a revolving loan fund and through negotiations with commercial banks and microfinance institutions.

(f) To engage in the processing and marketing of agricultural and aquatic products, including rice, yam, cassava, maize, soybeans, fish, and other commodities produced by members.

(g) To provide training and extension services to members in modern farming techniques, financial management, cooperative governance, and environmental stewardship.

(h) To undertake such other activities as may be conducive to the attainment of the foregoing objects, including the acquisition of land, vehicles, and equipment necessary for the Union's operations.

ARTICLE 4: VOTING, QUORUM, AND CONDUCT OF MEETINGS

(Note: This Article consolidates the original 2012 provisions with the amendments of 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2023. The text of each Section as set out below is the text currently in force.)

4.1 Right to Vote
(a) Each member society shall be entitled to one vote on every matter coming before the General Meeting, irrespective of the size of the society or the amount of its share capital.
(b) Voting shall be exercised by the authorised representative of the member society, whose name has been duly communicated to the Secretary General in accordance with Article 3.2(c).
(c) No member society shall be entitled to vote at any meeting if it is in arrears in the payment of any subscription, levy, or other sum due to the Union, provided that the Council of Delegates may, in its discretion and upon good cause shown, waive this disqualification for a particular meeting.
(d) Voting by proxy shall not be permitted. A member society unable to attend a meeting shall be deemed absent, and no other society or person may cast its vote.

4.2 Manner of Voting
(a) Voting shall ordinarily be by show of hands, unless a poll is demanded by the chairperson or by at least five member societies present and entitled to vote.
(b) Where a poll is demanded, it shall be taken by secret ballot in such manner as the chairperson may direct, and the result of the poll shall be declared by the chairperson and recorded in the minutes.
(c) For the election of officers and for any resolution amending this Constitution, voting shall be by secret ballot.
(d) A declaration by the chairperson that a resolution has been carried, or carried by a particular majority, shall be conclusive evidence of that fact, unless a poll is demanded in accordance with subsection (a) of this Section.

4.3 Quorum
(a) The quorum for a General Meeting shall be one-third of the member societies entitled to vote, present in person or by authorised representative.
(b) The quorum for a meeting of the Council of Delegates shall be one-half of the members of the Council.
(c) If within one hour after the time appointed for a meeting a quorum is not present, the meeting shall stand adjourned to the same day in the following week at the same time and place, or to such other day, time, and place as the chairperson may determine. At the adjourned meeting, the members present shall form a quorum, provided that not less than ten member societies are present.
(d) If at any meeting a quorum ceases to be present during the proceedings, the meeting may continue to receive reports and to adjourn, but shall not transact any other business.

4.4 Motions and Seconding
(a) No motion, other than a motion of procedure, shall be put to a meeting unless it has been seconded.
(b) A motion which is not seconded shall not be debated and shall be deemed to have lapsed.
(c) The proposer and the seconder of a motion shall be members entitled to vote at the meeting.
(d) An amendment to a motion may be moved, and if seconded, shall be debated and voted upon before the substantive motion is put.
(e) The chairperson may, with the consent of the meeting, accept a motion for the closure of debate. Such a motion shall be put to the meeting without debate and shall require a two-thirds majority of the votes cast.

4.5 Minutes and Records
(a) The Secretary General shall cause proper minutes to be kept of all proceedings of General Meetings and of meetings of the Council of Delegates.
(b) Minutes of each meeting shall be circulated to member societies within thirty days of the meeting, and shall be confirmed, amended, or rejected at the next meeting of the same body.
(c) A member society may, by written request to the Secretary General, have access to the minutes of any General Meeting, provided that the Council may restrict access to minutes or parts of minutes which, in its opinion, relate to matters of a confidential nature.

CONSTITUTION AND BYLAWS OF THE BENUE RIVER BASIN COOPERATIVE UNION

(Adopted at the Inaugural General Meeting, 14 April 2012; as amended through the
Extraordinary General Meeting of 18 March 2023)

---

ARTICLE 5: AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION AND BYLAWS

5.1 Right to Propose Amendments

(a) Any member society may propose an amendment to this Constitution or to the
Bylaws by submitting a written notice to the Secretary General at least sixty (60)
days before the date of the General Meeting at which the amendment is to be
considered.

(b) The Council of Delegates may likewise propose amendments, either on its own
initiative or upon the petition of not fewer than five member societies.

(c) Each proposal shall set out the exact wording of the article or section sought
to be amended, the reasons for the amendment, and the names and signatures of the
proposer and the seconder.

5.2 Circulation of Proposals

(a) Upon receipt of a valid proposal, the Secretary General shall circulate the
full text of the proposed amendment, together with the names of the proposer and
seconder, to all member societies not later than forty-five (45) days before the
General Meeting.

(b) The notice shall also indicate whether the Council of Delegates recommends
the adoption or rejection of the proposed amendment, or offers no recommendation.

(c) No amendment shall be considered at a General Meeting unless it has been
circulated in accordance with this section, unless the meeting by a two-thirds
majority of the votes cast suspends this requirement for reasons of urgency.

5.3 Adoption of Amendments

(a) An amendment to this Constitution shall be adopted only if it is approved by
a two-thirds majority of the votes cast by member societies present and voting at
a General Meeting.

(b) An amendment to the Bylaws shall require a simple majority of the votes
cast, except that an amendment to the Bylaws concerning the levying of dues or
the expulsion of a member society shall require a two-thirds majority.

(c) Voting shall be by secret ballot if so demanded by not fewer than one-third
of the member societies present.

(d) An amendment shall take effect immediately upon its adoption, unless the
resolution adopting it specifies a later date.

5.4 Review of the Constitution

(a) The Council of Delegates shall cause a full review of this Constitution and
the Bylaws to be undertaken at intervals of not more than five years.

(b) The review shall be conducted by a Constitution Review Committee appointed
by the Council, comprising not fewer than five persons, of whom at least three
shall be representatives of member societies.

(c) The Committee shall report to the Council, and the Council shall table the
report, together with its recommendations, at the next General Meeting.

5.5 Repeal and Replacement

(a) A proposal to repeal this Constitution and replace it with a new constitution
shall be treated as an amendment for the purposes of this Article, and shall
require a two-thirds majority of the votes cast at a General Meeting.

(b) The notice of such a proposal shall be accompanied by the full text of the
proposed new constitution.

---

ARTICLE 6: DISPUTE RESOLUTION

6.1 Objectives and Scope

(a) The Union shall seek to resolve all disputes arising between member
societies, between a member society and the Union, or between the Union and any
third party, by amicable means in the first instance.

(b) This Article shall not apply to disputes between individual members of a
member society, which shall be dealt with under the internal rules of that
society.

Membership recorded a net increase during the year. We commenced the year with 1,240 registered members and ended with 1,312, a growth of 72 members (5.8%). This is slightly below the 8% target we set in the 2022 work plan, largely due to the slow start of the maize off-season programme which delayed recruitment in some communities.

The suspension of 22 members was for non-compliance with the input repayment schedule. The disciplinary committee reviewed each case; 14 of those suspended have since paid and will be presented for reinstatement at the next general meeting. The remaining 8 are in active discussion with the committee.

We ran three membership drives: two in the eastern zone of the local government area and one in the north. The northern drive was less successful than anticipated, and the board will review the approach for 2023. We also introduced a referral incentive (₦500 per successful new member) in the third quarter, which accounted for roughly half of the new memberships.

**7. Oil Palm Production**

Oil palm remains a secondary but growing activity for the cooperative. We have 214 hectares under oil palm cultivation across three plantation sites. Of this, 148 hectares are mature and were harvested during the year, with the remaining 66 hectares being young plantings that are not yet in full production.

| Item | Quantity |
|---|---|
| Fresh fruit bunches (FFB) harvested | 1,940 tonnes |
| Crude palm oil (CPO) produced | 388 tonnes |
| Palm kernel produced | 97 tonnes |
| Average CPO extraction rate | 20% |

The extraction rate of 20% is within the expected range for our age of palms, though slightly below the 22% we achieved in 2021. The decline is attributed to the heavy rains in August which caused some fruit to be delivered late to the processing shed. The board has noted this and will adjust the harvest schedule in 2023 to avoid the worst of the wet season.

The palm oil was sold locally to traders from Makurdi and as far as Enugu. A small quantity (about 12 tonnes) was supplied to the BRBCU processing hub for blending in their soap production trial. The trial was successful and they have indicated an interest in a standing order for 2023, subject to price negotiations.

**8. Training and Extension**

We held a total of 14 training sessions during the year, reaching 386 members (including 214 women). The sessions covered:

- Improved cassava planting techniques (3 sessions)
- Oil palm estate management and harvesting best practice (2 sessions)
- Financial literacy and savings mobilisation (4 sessions)
- Pest and disease identification and control (2 sessions)
- Cooperative governance and member rights (3 sessions)

The financial literacy sessions were particularly well attended, and we have seen a 15% increase in member savings deposits in our internal savings scheme. Two of the governance sessions were held jointly with the na-Ala Cassava Growers Society, as part of our ongoing inter-society cooperation. This sharing of resources was cost-effective and will be continued.

A challenge we faced was the lack of a dedicated training officer. Our secretary doubled as the trainer for most sessions, which limited the number of sessions we could run. We have requested support from the BRBCU extension team for 2023.

**ANNUAL REPORT FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST DECEMBER 2022**

**January 2023**

**9. Grain Production and Storage**

The grain sub-programme covers maize, soybean, and sorghum grown by our members on their individual plots and aggregated through the society for marketing. This year was a mixed one for grains. The early rains were good and planting was completed on time across most member farms. However, the dry spell in late June affected maize flowering in the low-lying areas, and we saw some reduction in cob fill as a result.

| Crop | Area Planted (ha) | Production (tonnes) | Average Yield (t/ha) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maize | 212 | 318 | 1.50 |
| Soybean | 96 | 110 | 1.15 |
| Sorghum | 74 | 96 | 1.30 |

*Note: Area figures are as reported by members during the pre-planting survey in April 2022. Production figures are from the society's purchase records at the collection centre. Some members sold directly to local buyers without going through the society, so total production may be higher than shown here.*

The maize yield of 1.50 t/ha is below our target of 1.80 t/ha. The main causes were the June dry spell and a localised outbreak of fall armyworm in the Mbayion area. We distributed 40 litres of recommended pesticide to affected members, but some fields were already damaged. The soybean crop did well, with yields close to the expected range. Sorghum was planted mainly on the poorer soils and performed as expected.

**10. Storage and Marketing**

We have two community storage facilities: the main warehouse at the society compound in Gboko town (capacity 250 tonnes) and a smaller annex at the Mkar junction (capacity 80 tonnes). Both were in use throughout the year.

| Facility | Capacity (t) | Used for Maize (t) | Used for Soybean (t) | Used for Sorghum (t) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Main warehouse | 250 | 180 | 40 | 35 |
| Mkar annex | 80 | 50 | 15 | 10 |

The main warehouse was at 92% of capacity during the peak storage month of November. This was tight, and we had to turn away some members' produce. We have since discussed with the BRBCU about using their transit shed at the Makurdi depot for overflow in 2023. The annex at Mkar was less utilised, mainly because of its distance from the main collection route.

Storage losses were estimated at 3% overall, which we consider acceptable. The main loss was from weevils in the maize stored in the main warehouse during the hot months. We treated the grain with approved chemicals before storage, but the treatment was applied later than ideal for some batches. The board has recommended that we purchase a small mechanical drier to reduce moisture content before storage, which should cut losses further.

**Marketing**

We sold the bulk of our grain through the society's collective marketing arrangement. The prices we obtained are summarised below:

| Crop | Quantity Sold (t) | Average Price (₦/t) | Buyer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maize | 210 | 195,000 | BRBCU / Makurdi traders |
| Soybean | 95 | 250,000 | Feed millers, Kaduna |
| Sorghum | 80 | 160,000 | Breweries, Jos |

The maize price of ₦195,000 per tonne was higher than the 2021 price of ₦170,000. This was due to the general rise in food prices in the country. The soybean price was also strong. We were able to negotiate a slightly better rate for the soybean by delivering in bulk to a single buyer. The sorghum price was stable.
